questions.question: What parts of the ear are caused to vibrate when a sound wave enters?
options: Only the eardrum and the brain
The eardrum, the tiny bones inside the ear, and the cochlea
Just the auditory nerve and the outer ear lobe
Only the specialized cells in the brain

questions.question: What is the role of the specialized cells inside the cochlea?
options: To block loud noises from entering the brain
To vibrate the tiny bones of the middle ear
To sense vibrations and send electrical signals along a nerve to the brain
To pump fluid to the outer ear to keep it clean

questions.question: Which frequency range represents the normal limits of human hearing, and where is it most sensitive?
options: 20 Hz to 20 kHz, being most sensitive to 2-5 kHz
10 Hz to 10 kHz, being most sensitive to 1-2 kHz
50 Hz to 50 kHz, being most sensitive to 10-15 kHz
200 Hz to 20,000 kHz, being most sensitive to 5-10 kHz

questions.question: When a sound wave travels through the air, how do the individual air particles behave?
options: They travel continuously forward with the wave from the source to the listener
They spin in small circles without any back-and-forth movement
They vibrate parallel to the direction of the wave travel, rather than travelling forward
They vibrate up and down at a 90-degree angle to the wave's path

questions.question: Why is sound classified as a longitudinal wave?
options: Because the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
Because the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Because it can travel through a vacuum like light waves
Because it travels slower in solids than in gases

questions.question: Why do sound waves travel faster in solids than in liquids?
options: Because solids have larger gaps between particles than liquids
Because the strong forces between particles in solids allow vibrations to travel even faster
Because solids are always warmer than liquids
Because particles in a solid travel along with the sound wave

questions.question: Which of the following is the approximate speed of sound in air, and how does it compare to its speed in other states of matter?
options: About 340 m/s, being faster in liquids and faster still in solids
About 300,000,000 m/s, being slower in liquids and solids
About 1500 m/s, being slower in solids but faster in liquids
About 340 m/s, being slower in liquids and slowest in solids

questions.question: What happens when a sound wave reflects off a hard surface and is heard again?
options: It undergoes refraction and becomes high-pitched
It creates an echo
It is absorbed and disappears completely
It turns into a transverse wave

questions.question: A sound wave travels 680 meters in 2 seconds. What equation is used to find its speed?
options: speed = distance + time
speed = distance * time
speed = distance / time
speed = time / distance

questions.question: Why is it beneficial to measure longer distances and times when designing an experiment to find the speed of sound?
options: It completely eliminates all sources of human reaction time
Any errors become a smaller proportion of the overall measurements
It causes the speed of sound to increase, making it easier to record
It changes the sound wave from longitudinal to transverse

questions.question: Which statement is true regarding the safety and physical effect of ultrasound waves on the human body?
options: They cause harmful cell mutations because they carry ionizing radiation
They can cause objects to vibrate and transfer energy, but do not harm the human body
They damage tissues by raising body temperature to dangerous levels
They cannot transfer any energy to physical structures

questions.question: How is ultrasound used to create images of structures inside the human body?
options: It ionizes the tissues to reveal their chemical makeup
It reflects from the boundaries between different types of body tissues
It passes straight through all tissues without any reflection
It converts the body tissues into light-emitting sources

questions.question: Describe the motion of a small portion of water as a water wave passes through it.
options: It travels forward across the surface along with the wave crest
It moves up and down (oscillates) rather than moving forward
It sinks to the bottom of the pool and stays there
It moves in a continuous straight line in the opposite direction of the wave

questions.question: Why are water waves classified as transverse waves?
options: Because the direction of oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Because the direction of oscillation is at 90 degrees to the direction of energy transfer
Because they can travel through a complete vacuum
Because they carry matter rather than energy

questions.question: What is wave superposition?
options: The process of a wave changing its frequency as it enters a new medium
The bending of waves as they pass around a sharp barrier
The effect where waves passing through each other can 'add up' or 'cancel out'
The complete loss of energy as a wave travels over a long distance
